title: ST-HHOL: Spatio-Temporal Hierarchical Hypergraph Online Learning for Crime Prediction
claim: Crime patterns differ by context and time, and shift unpredictably across space and days, so static models fail.
layout: 2 panels: paired map snapshots left, five-day heatmap series right
description: Panel (a) shows two real map screenshots side by side. The left one is a night scene with a moon icon, marked with bar icons and assault gun icons. The right one is a daytime scene with a sun icon, marked with subway station icons and theft briefcase icons. A legend below lists Bar, Assault, Subway Station and Theft. Panel (b) shows five Chicago community-area choropleth maps for 2024-06-01 to 2024-06-05, colored with a yellow-to-purple-to-black scale from 0 to 7 crime count. White-bordered regions mark areas whose counts change sharply from day to day. A vertical colorbar labeled Crime count sits at the far right. The eye goes first to the dark, saturated hotspots in the maps.
caption: (a) Example of the heterogeneity of latent crime patterns: assaults near nightlife at midnight, thefts near subways in daytime. (b) Spatial distribution of “Criminal Damage” in Chicago (June 1–5, 2024), with the white-bordered region indicating non-stationarity.
abstract: Crime prediction is a critical yet challenging task in urban spatio-temporal forecasting. Sparse crime records alone are insufficient to capture latent high-order patterns shaped by heterogeneous contextual factors with spatial and criminal specificity, while high non-stationarity renders conventional offline models ineffective against concept drift. To tackle these challenges, we propose a Spatio-Temporal Hierarchical Hypergraph Online Learning framework named ST-HHOL. First, we propose a hierarchical hypergraph convolution network that integrates crime data with heterogeneous contextual factors to uncover dual-specific crime patterns and their co-occurrence relations. Second, we introduce an iterative online learning strategy to address concept drift by employing frequent fine-tuning for short-term dynamics and periodic retraining for long-term shifts. Moreover, we adopt a Partially-Frozen LLM that leverages pre-trained sequence priors while adapting its attention mechanisms to crime-specific dependencies, enhancing spatio-temporal reasoning under sparse supervision. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that ST-HHOL consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy and robustness, while also providing enhanced interpretability. Code is available at https://github.com/777Rebecca/ST-HHOL.
